PASSO 1: «querer» é querer. É um verbo i: STEP 1: «querer» means to want. It's an irregular verb, but with an easy pattern: in four forms the stem's «e» becomes «ie», and in «nosotros» and «vosotros» it stays «e». «Quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren.» STEP 2: to order, pair «querer» with a noun: «Quiero un café», «Queremos dos zumos». STEP 3: «Quiero…» is direct and fine among friends, but can sound blunt with strangers. Better is «Quisiera…»: «Quisiera un café con leche, por favor». Learn «quisiera» as a ready-made phrase — it's more polite, and its grammar comes much later. STEP 4: always add «por favor» and «gracias». STEP 5: the waiter (in Spain, «camarero») asks: «¿Qué desea?» (usted) or «¿Qué quieres?» (tú). Another question is «¿Qué va a tomar?», and the natural answer is «Para mí, un café». STEP 6: «tomar» means to eat or to drink, so «¿Qué va a tomar?» isn't only about drinks. STEP 7: use «con» and «sin» to adjust your order: «un café con leche», «un té sin azúcar», «un zumo con hielo». STEP 8: Latin America has its own variants: «jugo» instead of «zumo», «mesero» or «mozo» instead of «camarero», and «torta» or «sándwich» instead of «bocadillo», depending on the country. Learn Spain's words and recognize the others. STEP 9: water is «el agua» — use «el» in the singular because of the stressed «a» sound (lesson 5), but «el agua fría» and «las aguas». Ask for «un vaso de agua» or «una botella de agua».
em português dizemos «eu queria um café»: English «I'd like a coffee» is exactly the function «quisiera» serves — a ready-made polite form, more polite than «quiero» (I want). The waiter's question matches too: «¿Qué desea?» is literally «what do you desire?», the Spanish equivalent of a polite «what would you like?». The most common false friend at the table is «exquisito», which means delicious, not «weird» or «bizarre» (that's «raro» or «extraño»).

Contar de 20 a 100 e dizer preços: Counting from 20 to 100 and saying prices
PASSO 1: de 20 a 29, o espanhol escreve: STEP 1: from 20 to 29, Spanish writes it as a single word: «veinte, veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés, veinticuatro, veinticinco, veintiséis, veintisiete, veintiocho, veintinueve». Watch the accent marks in veintidós, veintitrés and veintiséis. STEP 2: the tens are: treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa, cien. STEP 3: from 31 to 99, write ten + «y» + unit, as three words: «treinta y uno», «cuarenta y cinco», «noventa y nueve». STEP 4: «uno» drops the «o» before a masculine noun and becomes «un»: «treinta y un euros»; before a feminine noun, it becomes «una»: «veintiuna personas». And «veintiuno» becomes «veintiún»: «veintiún euros». STEP 5: «cien» means one hundred. Before a noun, and when it's exactly 100, use «cien»: «cien euros». For 101 to 199, Spanish uses «ciento»: «ciento uno». STEP 6: to say prices in euros, Spain uses «euros» and «céntimos»: «Son tres euros con cincuenta» (€3.50). Say the decimal point as «con». STEP 7: useful questions: «¿Cuánto es?» (the total bill), «¿Cuánto cuesta?» (the price of one item) and «¿Cuánto cuestan?» (the price of several). STEP 8: the «c» and «z» are pronounced with a «th» sound (in Spain) in «cincuenta» (theen-KWEN-tah) and «cien» (thee-EN). In Latin America, that sound is an «s». STEP 9: to say the total naturally, use «Son…» plus the amount. Don't use «Es» with more than one euro: «Son tres euros».
os números em português e espanhol são m: Spanish and English numbers work much the same way, but the writing differs. From 21 to 29, Spanish fuses everything into one word («veintiuno»); from 31 to 99, it's written as three words («treinta y uno») — like English «thirty-one», but with «y» (and) as a separate word instead of a hyphen. The small trap: never skip the «y» between the tens and the units.

Falsos amigos da mesa e frases de serviç: False friends at the table, and service phrases
PASSO 1: o primeiro falso amigo da mesa: STEP 1: the first false friend at the table is «vaso»: in Spanish it's the drinking glass for water («un vaso de agua»); for a flower pot, it's «maceta». STEP 2: «taza» is the cup; «copa» is a wine or dessert glass, and also the trophy in a tournament. STEP 3: «cena» means dinner: «la cena es a las nueve» (clock time comes in the next lesson). It's not a scene from a movie, which is «escena». STEP 4: «cola» means a line/queue: «hacer cola» means to stand in line. The same word «cola» also means an animal's tail, and glue. STEP 5: «exquisito» means delicious or refined: «una paella exquisita». What's weird in Spanish is «raro» or «extraño». STEP 6: «propina» means a tip; in Spain it's usually small and optional, and customs vary from country to country. STEP 7: service phrases: «una mesa para dos, por favor», «la carta, por favor» (the menu, also «el menú»), «¿Qué recomienda?», «está muy rico» (it's really tasty — «rico» in this sense is very common), «¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor?». STEP 8: Spain has a fixed-price «menú del día»: a set price with a starter, a main course, and dessert, mostly at lunchtime. STEP 9: «la cuenta» is the check, and you ask the waiter for it once you're done.
este quadro reúne os falsos amigos que m: This set gathers the false friends that trip people up most at the table. «Vaso» isn't a vase, «cena» isn't a movie scene, «cola» isn't a cola drink, and «exquisito» doesn't mean odd. If you say «una cena exquisita», you mean a delicious dinner, not a strange one.
